Based on my reading the reviews, author responses and discussion, I see the following strengths of this manuscript:

- **S1.** The submission focuses on an underexplored area of the routing scheme in IVF based max-inner-product-search or MIPS, and proposes a new routing scheme that results in significant reduction of the number of points that need to be probed.

- **S2.** The presentation is very clear, and the proposed scheme is well positioned against existing literature on similarity (both in the original submission and in the author-reviewer discussion).

I also see the following limitations of this manuscript:

- **L1.** One significant limitation appears to be the specific focus on IVF based schemes, as that can limit the impact of the proposed scheme. However, the authors have attempted to address this concern in the author response by highlighting situations where IVF based schemes are the right way to go, and the proposed scheme would provide benefits in such situations.

- **L2.** Another limitation appears to be the empirical evaluation that focuses on the number of points probed as a surrogate for latency. However, in the response to reviewers, the authors provide evidence that this metric is an appropriate surrogate for latency, thereby justifying their choice.

I believe while this paper has limitations, the limitations have been appropriately addressed through the author-reviewer discussion.

Thank you for engaging in a good faith discussion with us and for keeping an open mind! We appreciate the conversation and the discussion of these subtle points which will ultimately help us clarify or articulate sources of confusion in the article.

If we may ask a follow up question to better understand your concerns and perhaps offer a solution: Would you mind articulating why you believe our evaluation protocol is inadequate? We'd in particular be grateful if you could give us an example of when our evaluation of latency by proxy (plus real-world experiments using a system with Blob storage and PQ scoring) can lead to a different conclusion than a recall-latency curve as you suggest.

We strongly believe our evaluation methodology is an elegant way to formalize latency in such a way that is independent of I/O bandwidth, the specific choice of scoring, and CPU type and number of threads. There is a one-to-one mapping between how much data one router saves versus another, and the fetch and scoring latencies.

As a final note, we completely agree that a work that is developing a new ANN search algorithm could and should include a recall-latency curve. That is necessary so that one can fairly compare one algorithm from one class (say IVF) against algorithms from other classes (e.g., graphs, LSH, trees).

In our case, we are only comparing one router against other routers, within the same framework. If routing algorithm A decides it needs 50% less data to reach the same accuracy as routing algorithm B, then the savings propagate to other stages of IVF (fetch and scoring). However, as we show, how much that saving matters depends on the hardware (and choice of scoring function).

Our bottom line is that: Optimist is not always a good choice. Whether it's appropriate or not depends heavily on hardware, storage medium, and scoring algorithms. For instance, Optimist is not a reasonable choice if the index is entirely in memory.

Thank you for reading our rebuttal and for your note!

> This paper still does not clarify why this is worth investigating

While we understand your argument, we do not agree that this question is in-scope for our study. We believe IVF is worth investing research in because it is widely adopted for a multitude of reasons, including index construction time (e.g., using KMeans on a small sample of a dataset), disk access pattern predictability (due to contiguous storage of vectors in the same cluster), and advanced quantization methods (e.g., residual PQ). Its adoption in industry, using the precise disk-based setup, should speak to its merits (c.f., https://turbopuffer.com/blog/turbopuffer and https://www.pinecone.io/blog/serverless-architecture/#Pinecone-serverless-architecture)

In summary, whether IVF or graph indices are right an application depend not just on their query-time performance but also on other constraints such as memory usage, I/O usage, ease of caching, quantization, etc. That is why we do not believe it is within the scope of our study to argue for or against two major, widely adopted ANN search paradigms.

> ... DiskANN obtains high recall within 10 ms on billion-scale datasets.

Again, we do not claim one is better than the other. Sure, DiskANN can be faster at query time (as it has a logarithmic time complexity in the number of vectors), but its index is more expensive to build. As a word of caution, "10ms/query with a high recall on billion-scale dataset" is not an entirely accurate statement: latency depends on the number and type of CPUs used, SSD vs BLOB storage, memory bandwidth, among other factors.

> [$\delta$] needs a discussion that introduces a setting without probability, explains a solution, and then analyzes its success probability.

We explain how $\delta$ should be interpreted on Lines 122-132. We analyze its effect in practice in Figure 7.

$\delta$ is a hyperparameter with an intuitive interpretation. This is similar to `ef_search` in HNSW. Or $\alpha$ is DiskANN. We don't think DiskANN's $\alpha$ is more interpretable than our $\delta$, or vice versa. It is just a hyperparameter whose value depends on the application and dataset.

> This should be included in the main body of this paper.

Thank you for inquiring about the time complexity! We'll be sure to include this analysis in our revised draft.

> However, routing, fetch, and scoring have different time complexities.

One of the challenges with measuring latency is that it is hard to understand, let alone reproduce. The reason being that latency depends on the hardware itself (I/O bandwidth, layers of caching in CPU or RAM, the CPU itself, number of threads). If we just presented latencies and stated a number such as 10ms/query, a) we ourselves wouldn't be able to replicate the study precisely and b) a reader with access to vastly different hardware cannot confidently assess what the latency will be like if they replicated our study.

That brings us to our method of evaluation that is not only reproducible, but it also paints a better picture for comparing different methods. A good way to understand it is as follows:

Figure 2 shows the relative (among different routers) amount of data points that need to be probed to reach a certain recall. This is a proxy to a) the number of clusters one needs to fetch and b) the number of points one needs to score. What does that entail? If we look at Figure 2(c):
- Optimist(2, .8) reaches a recall of 0.975 by probing roughly 1.25% of the dataset. Subpartition (and Mean) reach about the same recall by probing a little more than 2%.
- This tells us that Optimist requires us to fetch about 37% less data (0.75% of the dataset) from secondary storage
- That amount can be translated into fetch latency savings given your specific I/O bandwidth
- This also translates into scoring latency savings given your specific CPU (and number of threads) for example.

The numbers above do not reflect the routing latency. So here is what we offered instead:
- We will include theoretical routing time complexity (during search) in a revised draft. For Mean and the like, it's simply $\mathcal{O}(Ld)$. For Subpartition and Optimist, it is $\mathcal{O}(Ldt)$
- We included Figure 3 to show that under what circumstances an increased routing latency ($\mathcal{O}(Ltd)$ vs $\mathcal{O}(Ld)$) is justified: When fetching data from storage is expensive (BLOB, e.g.), then the amount of time spent on routing is dwarfed by the fetch latency. That's a setting we believe our method is more appropriate for.

As a final note, we'd like to add that routing, fetch, and scoring latencies are independent. Scoring can be done by PQ or delegated to a graph sub-index for the fetched partitions. Fetch latency depends on the storage medium and the bandwidth. Routing depends on the CPU and memory configuration. It is impractical to measure end-to-end latencies for all possible combinations of these components.

Thank you for taking the time to review our work and give us your thoughts on the current draft! We also appreciate the in-depth questions. We have included below a note with responses to your questions. We hope that clarifies some of the points and resolves some of your concerns.

> Q1: Why did this work consider an IVF-based algorithm? It is well known that IVF-based algorithms were outperformed by graph-based algorithms (e.g., DiskANN [Subramanya et al., 2019]). I agree that IVF-based algorithms are easy to fit into the disk-based setting, but this is not specific to IVF. You can see that DiskANN can deal with MIPS (https://github.com/microsoft/DiskANN), so the authors need to use it as a baseline. From that paper, DiskANN can obtain high recall (e.g., 95%) within about 5 milliseconds on Deep1B, while OPTIMIST took more on Deep10M. This paper does not claim the merit of IVF compared to the other approaches successfully and thus fails to motivate the IVF work.

IVF and graph-based approaches to ANN search are two prominent paradigms that are widely adopted in practice. There are many examples of both of these in the (still very much active) academic literature as well as industry solutions. We cited some that speak to both, and why one may choose IVF over graphs and vice versa. But if you find those references insufficient, a very recent study [Kuffo and Boncz “Bang for the Buck: Vector Search on Cloud CPUs”] performs a comparative analysis and explains why one may adopt IVF over graphs and vice versa.

Our work is a study of routing in IVF, a subproblem that is specific to IVF. We do not claim IVF is “better” than graphs in any shape or form, and have no qualms about whether one chooses DiskANN or IVF in practice. The problem we studied is an underexplored research topic within the IVF method, and we show there is room for research. To give you an analogy, the equivalent problem in DiskANN (or graph methods in general) is how to traverse the graph; the current practice is a greedy search. Our research presented in this work is equivalent to research on other ways of traversing the graph during search. We therefore do not agree that a comparison with DiskANN adds any value whatsoever to the merits or conclusions of our work.

> Q2: Section 2.1 uses the $(1 + \delta) / 2$  success probability as its objective without justification. From the application perspective, it is hard to understand why this probability is involved in the problem setting. Clearly, this setting is derived from the theoretical bounding procedure, and it is not convincing why we need to address Problem 1. This work needs a more convincing setting.

Section 1 Subsection “Existing routers and the role of optimism” shows why we hypothesize that the principle of optimism plays a role in the efficacy of routing in IVF. That motivated us to formalize the notion of optimism for IVF, which is our definition presented in Problem 1. We do not claim that Problem 1 is the only way to formalize that notion; we instead offer it as a reasonable definition of optimism: Depending on how much information is available to us, we can, with some confidence (i.e., $(1 + \delta)/2$) estimate that the probability of the maximum inner product within a shard is no greater than a threshold ($\theta_i$). A larger $\delta$ makes the formulation more optimistic. This message should come across in the discussion that immediately follows Problem 1 (Lines 122 through 129).

As for why $(1 + \delta) / 2$: The choice is for notation purposes only. The expression was chosen to (a) allow $\delta$ to be between 0 and 1, and (b) make expression (6) “cleaner.” You are free to change the right-hand-side of the inequality to $\delta$ in Problem 1, and that would simply change the expression in (6), nothing less, nothing more.

As for how one should interpret $\delta$ in practice: We have included extensive experiments that study this hyperparameter. Please see Figure 7 in Appendix E.

> Q3: In my understanding, the general solution (in Section 2.2) is not available in practice because it uses unknown distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . Section 2.3 overcomes this issue by ignoring the data distribution, which is good. My concern here is that, in both cases, the pre-processing needs more computational cost than the original IVF. However, its (BuildRouterForPartition's) cost has not been analyzed theoretically and empirically. Because eigendecomposition requires a high computational cost (i.e., $\mathcal{O}(nd^2 + d^3)$  for  matrix), the pre-processing would incur a high cost for high-dimensional vectors.

You are correct in noticing that when computed using naive algorithms, the time complexity of the algorithm is dominated by the eigendecomposition step which takes $\mathcal{O}(nd^2 + d^3)$ time. However, as highlighted in our response to reviewer oyGp, since we only need the top $t$ eigenvectors and values to build the router, we can use highly-efficient algorithms designed to compute low-rank approximations of PSD matrices - such as the randomized Block Krylov Method. The survey by Tropp (2018) [1] gives an overview of these methods in Section 6.3 and Musco & Musco (2015) give a theoretical analysis of this algorithm. The time complexity of these algorithms is proportional to $\mathcal{O}(nd \log(d) * t)$ making them much faster than naive eigendecomposition. Since t is usually a small constant in our setting, Algorithm 1 can be implemented in near linear time complexity in the size of the data.

[1] Tropp, J. A. (2018). Analysis of randomized block Krylov methods.
[2] Musco, C., & Musco, C. (2015). Randomized block Krylov methods for stronger and faster approximate singular value decomposition. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (Vol. 2015‑January, pp. 1396–1404).


> Q4: The main experimental results show "recall and % points probed." The difference of #points probed however does not guarantee to show the difference of running time directly. Therefore, the authors need to use time-recall curves. In addition, comparing with state-of-the-art disk-based graph indices is missing.

This is a great question with an answer that is nuanced. Let us elaborate.

As we explain in the submission, there are three main subroutines that contribute to ANN search latency: (a) routing, (b) fetching, and (c) scoring. The routing latency is a function of the number of clusters. The fetch latency depends on the number of identified clusters, which in turn is proportional to the number of points in the union of those clusters. The scoring latency is a function of the number of points that need to be scored.

Following the reasoning above, it is appropriate to measure recall vs. the number of points probed. However, for completeness, in Figure 3, we provide a breakdown of the search time as a sum of its three main operations when indexes are on SSD or blob storage. The analysis is provided as mean latency (msec.) to reach 95% recall. In Appendix I, we extend the same analysis by introducing the number of threads used in a multi-threading search (1, 2, and 4 threads).

As for a comparison with disk-based graph indices, please see our response to Q1.

Thank you for your detailed review of our work! We appreciate your balanced feedback and your excellent questions. Below is our response to your questions and concerns, but we hope to engage in a discussion should our note prove inadequate.

> Q1. Regarding the algorithm design, please explain how to support dynamic updates and conduct experiments on this practical issue.

We agree that addressing dynamic updates is an important, practical question. But the main question there is: How does one add points to existing clusters, and when does one create new clusters? That question is naturally orthogonal to how queries are routed. When a new cluster is formed, or a cluster is updated, all that must happen to route queries correctly is to update the routing logic for that cluster. In Mean or NormalizedMean routers, the centroid must be recalculated; in ScaNN, the weighted centroid must be recomputed; in Optimist, it’s the mean and covariance that must be estimated.

> Q2. Time complexity of Algorithm 1 should be analyzed.

When computed using naive algorithms, the time complexity of the algorithm is dominated by the eigendecomposition step which takes $\mathcal{O}(nd^2 + d^3)$ time. However, since we only need the top $t$ eigenvectors and values to build the router, we can use highly-efficient algorithms designed to compute low-rank approximations of PSD matrices - such as the randomized Block Krylov Method. The survey by Tropp (2018) [1] gives an overview of these methods in Section 6.3 and Musco & Musco (2015) give a theoretical analysis of this algorithm. The time complexity of these algorithms is proportional to $\mathcal{O}(n d \log(d) * t)$ making them much faster than naive eigendecomposition. Since $t$ is usually a small constant in our setting, Algorithm 1 can be implemented in near linear time complexity in the size of the data.

[1] Tropp, J. A. (2018). Analysis of randomized block Krylov methods.
[2] Musco, C., & Musco, C. (2015). Randomized block Krylov methods for stronger and faster approximate singular value decomposition. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (Vol. 2015‑January, pp. 1396–1404).

> Q3. Section 2.2 starts with an assumption of Gaussian distribution. To support this assumption, it may be better to present a figure on the data distribution.

Gaussian distribution is a toy example to ease our way into a discussion of the general solution. It’s an example of how moments can be used to find an exact solution to Problem 1. It has no other significance whatsoever.

> Q4. The evaluation mainly assesses recall. However, the major concern seems to be time efficiency. The results would be more convincing if the authors directly report the search time (ie latency as did in the appendix).

We report recall as a function of the number of data points probed to enable a fair comparison of the efficacy of different routers. The desiderata here is to show how our proposed router is able to decrease the number of points probed while keeping recall high. The evaluation in terms of data points is done to decouple it from possible imbalance in shard sizes, so that a router cannot trivially outperform another by simply prioritizing larger shards. The evaluation in terms of search time is done end-to-end, i.e., we consider the total time required by the search operation, which is the sum of routing, fetch, and scoring. We report the results in Figure 3. Full results about search time are in Appendix I. Please also see our response to Q4 from Reviewer uLpi

> Q5. Based on the experimental setup, it seems all compared methods must linearly scan each shard. However, in practice, each shard can be indexed by graph-based MIPS index (eg HNSW [R1]). Since HNSW is highly scalable, the improvement may become marginal when HNSW indexes each shard. Please conduct an additional experiment.

Whether or not each shard uses PQ to compute scores or IP-HNSW/any other graph algorithm to find the top-k from the shard is immaterial. Studying Figure 3 explains why: Most of the time spent processing a query is on fetching the data from disk, especially in the Blob storage setup, while scoring is a fraction of the total time. Replacing PQ with IP-HNSW (or any “faster” method) would only shrink the scoring time, making it an even smaller fraction of the total cost.

As you can see from the extent of experimental results reported throughout our work, we are not resistant to the idea of conducting additional experiments so long as they shed light on what we cannot definitively conclude from the current set of experiments. In this case, we can state the above definitively.


> Q6. In both the Introduction and Experimental Setup, the number of clusters is assumed to be $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$  without references for this setting. When handling many clusters, construction time may be slow. Please report the construction time.

We apologize for leaving out the references. Please see Section 5.1 (subsection “Setting the number of lists”) in Douze et al.’s “The Faiss Library.”  That work explains why $\sqrt{m}$ is a good choice. There are many subsequent studies that adopt that choice - which we’d be happy to list here if necessary.

> Q7. Some presentation issues:
(1) In the references, the venue for "Unleashing Graph Partitioning for Large-Scale Nearest Neighbor Search" should be reported.
(2) Discussion on the limitations of the proposed solution is missing.
(3) Overall, this paper may be a little hard to follow for readers without enough background knowledge.

Thank you for this feedback! We’ll be sure to address (1) and (2) in a revised draft. As for (3), if you have specific sections that you found confusing or not friendly to the uninitiated, we would gladly revise to make the work more accessible.

We appreciate your feedback and your recognition of the strengths of our work! We wish to give our response to your questions below, but please let us know should you have further questions or concerns.

> To remove the second assumption, would a random rotation as used, e.g., in the fast-JL transform work out of the box when applied to the data points?
> If the shards were not given as input, is there some hope to compute shards that provide better guarantees for Problem 1?

These are good suggestions. A random rotation or JL Transform could certainly be used out of the box in this algorithm  as a pe-processing step on the vectors. It could also work to remove this assumption - some care will be required in choosing the transform and proving the minimum bound on the entries since the JL transform bounds do not provide a bound on the minimum value of the entries; but, we believe that this is possible and a nice future contribution to this line of investigation.

One could potentially compute the shards by clustering points in a way that makes it more efficient to solve Problem 1 or makes it possible to solve it more accurately. There are a couple of obstacles with doing this however. One, it is not obvious what the right clustering loss function here is. Since Problem 1 is well-defined and can be solved independently of how the shards are computed, we need to decide how to “couple” the loss function and Problem 1. This is an interesting problem that deserves future investigation. Second, in production systems for ANN, building the index needs to be as efficient as possible - in IVF-based indexes, clustering is the most expensive part of this computation. Doing clustering using a more complicated loss function is likely to make this process much slower. That said, investigating this tradeoff is worth investigating in future work.

We appreciate your taking the time to carefully review our submission and your on-point questions! We have included below our response to the concerns you raised in your feedback, but would be happy to expand if necessary.

> Another algorithm this paper may want to compare against is the cover tree [Beygelzimer et. al. 2006], which performs exact nearest neighbor search using O(log m) query time, where m is the number of data points. It seems that the query time for this algorithm achieving approximate nearest neighbor search is on average O(C + m/C), where C is the number of shards. This is optimized to O(sqrt(m)). Of course, there may be real trade-offs between these two approaches, which might mean that the proposed approach is still viable in practice. Perhaps the authors could comment on when they think the proposed approach would have benefits? I can partially answer this question: the cover tree might not admit sharding. Also, the approaches might not be mutually exclusive (the cover tree data structure could be used within the shard, leading to an overall query complexity of O(C + log m / C), or the optimized O((log m)^{1/2})).

Let us unpack your question into its parts and answer them separately.

Cover Tree’s query time complexity: We’d like to make a very minor and rather tangential point first: The original paper by Beygelzimer, Kakade, and Langford (“Cover trees for nearest neighbor” ICML 2006) claims and proves that the query time is $\mathcal{O}(\log m)$. Many years later, in 2022, Elkin and Kurlin (“Counterexamples expose gaps in the proof of time complexity for cover trees introduced in 2006”) presented a counter-example, exposing a gap in the proof presented in the original work. In a follow-on work in ICML 2023 (“A New Near-linear Time Algorithm For k-Nearest Neighbor Search Using a Compressed Cover Tree”), the two authors rectified the algorithm so that it admits a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}((k+ \log m) \log k)$ where $k$ is the number of nearest neighbors to find.

Why LSH, Trees, Graphs, and IVF: The ANN literature is vast (c.f., Bruch “Foundations of Vector Retrieval”). The story began with LSH and Trees. Many of these methods have been adapted to high dimensionalities and modern hardware [Ram and Sinha, “Revisiting kd-tree for nearest neighbor search” 2019; Gu et al. “Parallel Cover Trees and their Applications” 2022; Lv et al. “Multi-Probe LSH: Efficient Indexing for High-Dimensional Similarity Search”]. Nonetheless, they struggle to scale in practice, either due to build-time complexity or query time complexity – constants in the big-O notation become too large in practice.

That is in fact why IVF and Graphs have become the focus of intense research in the ANN search literature, and have been widely adopted in practice. There is a very recent study that offers a comparative analysis speaking to why one would use IVF over graphs and vice versa [Kuffo and Boncz “Bang for the Buck: Vector Search on Cloud CPUs”]. We should note that, there are many other publications that support our statement that IVF and graphs are popular choices at scale; we cited some of them on the first page, along with links to blogs from industry researchers.

One particular advantage of IVF is exactly what you pointed out: Each shard can use whichever ANN search method suitable to the application setup to return its top-k points! That can be Product Quantization based score computation; a graph index such as HNSW or the Vamana graph; or LSH and Trees (including Cover Trees).

Comparison with other classes of ANN search algorithms: Our work is concerned with a particular subroutine within the IVF framework. The aim of our study is not to compare IVF with other methods, or the merits of IVF against other classes of algorithms. Instead, we show that the routing subroutine is underexplored and offer an insight and a solution to that particular problem.

Our contributions are only meaningful in the context of IVF, and are relevant to those who (for one reason or another) choose IVF as their method of performing ANN search. We are in no way opposed to conducting a comprehensive comparative analysis of IVF (w/ different routing functions) and other algorithms, but we find that to be a rather orthogonal question that either has been addressed in the past or is best addressed in a separate study.

We hope we were able to answer your questions. But if there are any points that remain unclear, we’d be delighted to address them.


> I think it would be reasonable to also study the case where the algorithm has control over how the shards are generated. For example, is there a large benefit if the shards are guaranteed to have bounded diameter (and so have subgaussian concentration)? Or, is it often the case that the router is constructed independently of the sharding process?

That’s an excellent question and one that is worth investigating in and of itself. Indeed, many existing routers are tied to clustering, which is the subroutine that generates the shards. Mean and NormalizedMean rise from standard and spherical KMeans respectively. ScaNN has its own clustering objective that is a modification of the KMeans iterative algorithm.

We isolated routing from clustering to remove a confounding variable: By fixing the shards themselves, we can directly compare the routing protocols. Had we allowed each router to dictate how the shards are produced, we would not have been able to perform an apples-to-apples comparison of routers.

Now, would it benefit Optimist if it had a say in how the shards are produced? First, each shard’s inner product distribution is subgaussian simply because it has bounded support. But that detail aside: It is likely that by modifying the clustering objective to align with Optimist’s routing logic (similar to what ScaNN does, for instance), its performance might improve or its covariance matrix might become sparser and thus more compact. We give a more detailed explanation of why we do not believe coupling Optimist to a clustering loss is a trivial problem in our response to Reviewer HqdC.

While we find that question fascinating, we believe the scope of the paper is to establish whether optimism, formalized as we do in Problem 1, offers any advantage in and of itself. Our study gives an affirmative answer to that question. Can we improve the algorithm now that we know it has merit? Of course! We do not claim this is the end of the road, and encourage research in this space. But we strongly believe that research would be more appropriate in a separate study.

We’d be happy to elaborate further should you find our response inadequate. 

> White it is fairly clear, it may be nice to have a brief but explicit section on the computational complexity of constructing, updating, and querying this data structure.

Thank you for the suggestion! Yes, we admit we should have included a note on that with proper time complexity analysis. Sorry. We will add that to a revised draft.

> See above section under weaknesses. I think it may be good to include discussion about the cover tree and related exact and ANN data structures. Currently, I will recommend a 4: Borderline Accept. I think the problem studied is quite interesting and is worth publishing for a simple solution. But there is a lot left that could be said that would be reasonable to expect this paper to include.

Thank you for your transparent reasoning for the recommended rating! We hope our answers to your questions above remedy some of your concerns. We’re happy to answer any further questions you may have to convey more clearly why we think our work offers lessons that should be shared with the research community.

summary.value:
Suppose that a large dataset is stored across many shards. The goal, given a query point, is to find the k nearest neighbor (or more specifically, the data points with the top k inner product with the query point). This paper studies the problem of routing, which is the problem of how to summarize the shards and choose which shards to look for the top k data points.

Prior approaches are to summarize each shard by the mean or normalized mean (unit vector) of the data points in the shard, and then search within shards whose mean has maximal inner product with the query point. This paper proposes a simple refinement, where what is stored in not just the mean of shard, but its covariance (or an approximation of it). Using a concentration inequality a la Chebyshev, it is possible to compute an estimate of how large the dot product of the query vector with the top data point in a shard is.

Another contribution that may be of independent interest was an efficient decomposition for PSD matrices as a sum of a diagonal matrix and a low rank matrix.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**

The paper studies a fundamental problem and provides a simple heuristic to solve it. It was also written pretty clearly, with nice intuition given throughout. I think this paper raises a problem area that is worth further research, especially motivated by how data is stored and queried in practice.

**Weaknesses**

I think the paper has sufficient material for publication, and worthwhile in that it points out a perhaps understudied problem that arises with extremely large-scale data. But I also think it leaves a lot of fairly obvious questions unanswered, and I think it is also reasonable if the paper were to be published in a future venue with more developed results. Some immediate points that come to mind:

1. Another algorithm this paper may want to compare against is the cover tree [Beygelzimer et. al. 2006], which performs exact nearest neighbor search using O(log m) query time, where m is the number of data points. It seems that the query time for this algorithm achieving approximate nearest neighbor search is on average O(C + m/C), where C is the number of shards. This is optimized to O(sqrt(m)). Of course, there may be real trade-offs between these two approaches, which might mean that the proposed approach is still viable in practice. Perhaps the authors could comment on when they think the proposed approach would have benefits? I can partially answer this question: the cover tree might not admit sharding. Also, the approaches might not be mutually exclusive (the cover tree data structure could be used within the shard, leading to an overall query complexity of O(C + log m / C), or the optimized O((log m)^{1/2})).

2. I think it would be reasonable to also study the case where the algorithm has control over how the shards are generated. For example, is there a large benefit if the shards are guaranteed to have bounded diameter (and so have subgaussian concentration)? Or, is it often the case that the router is constructed independently of the sharding process?

3. White it is fairly clear, it may be nice to have a brief but explicit section on the computational complexity of constructing, updating, and querying this data structure.

summary.value:
The paper studies clustering-based nearest neighbor search. Data structures for this purpose partition the data points into shards, and a query for a point $q$ proceeds in two steps: First, in a routing phase, a set of promising shards is selected. Second, inside each shard, a scoring mechanism is applied to identify the nearest neighbors.

The submission proposes a novel algorithm for the routing part (the first step above). The algorithm is based on the "principle of optimism" from online learning. In a nutshell, it takes an "optimism parameter" $\delta>0$ and assigns thresholds $\theta_i$ to shards such that with probability at least $(1+\delta)/2$ all data points in the shard have similarity at most $\theta_i$ with the query point.

The new algorithm is based on a one-sided Chebyshev inequality and then it is shown how it can be implemented more efficiently using low-rank approximation of the covariance matrix. This is achieved via SVD and via another, more efficient approach, that employs sketching. This method is motivated through multivariate Gaussians and some additional theoretical guarantees are derived.

In the experiments, the method is evaluated with data stored on SSDs and on blob storage. It is shown that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods substantially on different real-world datasets.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. Nearest neighbor search is an important and still highly active research topic.
2. The paper is very well-written and easy to follow.
3. The new method is well-motivated and easy to implement.
4. Theoretical guarantees are obtained. While I was initially a bit skeptical about the assumptions of Lemma 2, the appendix contains a short discussion about them. It also provides some properties of real-world datasets, showing the validity of the first assumption.

Weaknesses:
1. As pointed out in Appendix C.2, it might be possible to remove the second assumption through random rotations. I think this direction could have been explored a bit more (and it also does not seem overly difficult to me).

questions.value:
1. To remove the second assumption, would a random rotation as used, e.g., in the fast-JL transform work out of the box when applied to the data points?
2. If the shards were not given as input, is there some hope to compute shards that provide better guarantees for Problem 1?

**Strengths:**     
>S1. The paper studies a meaningful problem.  
>S2. The proposed solution has some new ideas.  
>S3. Experiments are conducted on multiple datasets.  

**Weaknesses:**  
>W1. Practical issues are not sufficiently considered in the algorithm design.  
>W2. Some experimental setups are unclear.

questions.value:
Q1. Regarding the algorithm design, please explain how to support dynamic updates and conduct experiments on this practical issue.

Q2. Time complexity of Algorithm 1 should be analyzed.

Q3. Section 2.2 starts with an assumption of Gaussian distribution. To support this assumption, it may be better to present a figure on the data distribution.

Q4. The evaluation mainly assesses recall. However, the major concern seems to be time efficiency. The results would be more convincing if the authors directly report the search time (ie latency as did in the appendix).

Q5. Based on the experimental setup, it seems all compared methods must linearly scan each shard. However, in practice, each shard can be indexed by graph-based MIPS index (eg HNSW [R1]). Since HNSW is highly scalable, the improvement may become marginal when HNSW indexes each shard. Please conduct an additional experiment.  
[R1] Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs. IEEE TPAMI.

Q6. In both the Introduction and Experimental Setup, the number of clusters is assumed to be $O(\sqrt{m})$ without references for this setting. When handling many clusters, construction time may be slow. Please report the construction time.

Q7. Some presentation issues:  
(1) In the references, the venue for "Unleashing Graph Partitioning for Large-Scale Nearest Neighbor Search" should be reported.  
(2) Discussion on the limitations of the proposed solution is missing.  
(3) Overall, this paper may be a little hard to follow for readers without enough background knowledge.

summary.value:
This paper considers the k-MIPS problem in the external memory setting.
The authors specifically focus on the IVF-based approach and proposed how to rank each cluster (or shard).
The representative existing approach computes the inner product of a given query and a cluster center for each cluster, and it accesses the $l$ clusters with the maximum inner products.
On the other hand, the proposed approach uses $\theta_i$ to estimate the maximum inner product obtained from $\mathcal{P}_i$ by considering its distribution.
The first practical solution requires $O(d^{2}|C|)$ space, which can be prohibitive for large $d$ and $|C|$.
Therefore, the authors proposed to approximate the covariance matrix to reduce the space to $O(t^{2}|C|)$ where $t \ll d$.
Under some assumption, the proposed sketch provides a lower error than Eckhart-Young-Mirsky Theorem.
Experiments were conducted on real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate that the proposed approach yields a better performance than the baseline approaches.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strong points
* The proposed routing is available for all IVF-based MIPS algorithms (generally).
* The proposed algorithm is designed from theory to practice.
* Experiments were conducted on real datasets.

Weak points
* It is well known that IVF-based algorithms are slower than graph-based ones.
* The setting of Problem 1 is arbitrary.
* Important experiments are missing.

questions.value:
- Q1: Why did this work consider an IVF-based algorithm?
It is well known that IVF-based algorithms were outperformed by graph-based algorithms (e.g., DiskANN [Subramanya et al., 2019]).
I agree that IVF-based algorithms are easy to fit into the disk-based setting, but this is not specific to IVF.
You can see that DiskANN can deal with MIPS (https://github.com/microsoft/DiskANN), so the authors need to use it as a baseline.
From that paper, DiskANN can obtain high recall (e.g., 95%) within about 5 milliseconds on Deep1B, while OPTIMIST took more on Deep10M.
This paper does not claim the merit of IVF compared to the other approaches successfully and thus fails to motivate the IVF work.

- Q2: Section 2.1 uses the $(1+\delta)/2$ success probability as its objective without justification.
From the application perspective, it is hard to understand why this probability is involved in the problem setting.
Clearly, this setting is derived from the theoretical bounding procedure, and it is not convincing why we need to address Problem 1.
This work needs a more convincing setting.

- Q3: In my understanding, the general solution (in Section 2.2) is not available in practice because it uses unknown distribution $\mathcal{D}$.
Section 2.3 overcomes this issue by ignoring the data distribution, which is good.
My concern here is that, in both cases, the pre-processing needs more computational cost than the original IVF.
However, its (BuildRouterForPartition's) cost has not been analyzed theoretically and empirically.
Because eigendecomposition requires a high computational cost (i.e., $O(nd^2 + d^3)$ for $n \times d$ matrix), the pre-processing would incur a high cost for high-dimensional vectors.

- Q4: The main experimental results show "recall and \% points probed."
The difference of #points probed however does not guarantee to show the difference of running time directly.
Therefore, the authors need to use time-recall curves.
In addition, comparing with state-of-the-art disk-based graph indices is missing.

title.value: Optimistic Query Routing in Clustering-based Approximate Maximum Inner Product Search

TLDR.value: We present an optimistic query routing protocol in clustering-based approximate maximum inner product search that reaches the same accuracy as SoTA routers by probing 50% fewer data points.

abstract.value: Clustering-based nearest neighbor search algorithms partition points into shards to form an index, and search only a subset of shards to process a query. Even though search efficacy is heavily influenced by the algorithm that identifies the shards to probe, it has received little attention in the literature. We study routing in clustering-based maximum inner product search, which includes cosine similarity search. We unpack existing routers and notice the surprising role of optimism. We then take a page from the sequential decision making literature and formalize that insight following the principle of ``optimism in the face of uncertainty.'' In particular, we present a framework that incorporates the moments of the distribution of inner products within each shard to estimate the maximum inner product. We then develop a practical instance of our algorithm that uses only the first two moments to reach the same accuracy as state-of-the-art routers by probing up to $50\%$ fewer points on benchmark datasets without compromising efficiency. Our algorithm is also space-efficient: we design a sketch of the second moment whose size is independent of the number of points and requires $\mathcal{O}(1)$ vectors per shard.
